policies.description: Alert when the Central secret is accessed.
policies.name: OpenShift: Central Admin Secret Accessed
policies.rationale: The Central secret can be used to login to the Central user interface as the admin user. This secret is generally salted and hashed by default in the data.htpasswd field, but may contain a base64 encoded password in the field data.password (if deployed with an Operator). This field may be safely removed. This secret should only be accessed for break glass troubleshooting and initial configuration. An update or access of this secret may indicate that it will be used to administer and configure security controls.
policies.remediation: Ensure that the Central admin secret was accessed for valid buiness purposes.

policies.description: Alert when the kubeadmin secret is accessed
policies.name: OpenShift: Kubeadmin Secret Accessed
policies.rationale: Kubeadmin is the default administrative user for OpenShift and can be used to obtain full administrative access to the cluster. Investigating if this was accessed for valid business purposes can help organizations to control the use of administrative privileges
policies.remediation: Audit the access carefully to ensure that this secret is only accessed for valid business purposes.

policies.description: Alert on deployments using an ADD command
policies.name: ADD Command used instead of COPY
policies.rationale: ADD incorporates a broader set of capabilities than COPY, including the ability to specify URLs as the source argument and automatic unpacking of compressed files onto the local filesystem. The effects of ADD can be unpredictable and can lead to larger images. Unless ADD's additional capabilities are required, COPY is recommended.
policies.remediation: Replace ADD with COPY when adding new files to the image. Per https://docs.docker.com/develop/develop-images/dockerfile_best-practices, it is better to use RUN curl instead of ADD if you need to access a URL.

policies.description: Alert on deployments that use the emergency annotation (e.g. "admission.stackrox.io/break-glass": "ticket-1234") to circumvent StackRox Admission Controller checks
policies.name: Emergency Deployment Annotation
policies.rationale: Ideally, all deployments should be validated before they are launched into the cluster; however, in case of emergency, annotations in the form of { "admission.stackrox.io/break-glass": "ticket-1234"} can be used to avoid those checks.
policies.remediation: Redeploy your service and unset the emergency annotation.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with the Alpine Linux package manager (apk) present
policies.name: Alpine Linux Package Manager (apk) in Image
policies.rationale: Package managers make it easier for attackers to use compromised containers, since they can easily add software.
policies.remediation: Run `apk --purge del apk-tools` in the image build for production containers.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with components of the Debian/Ubuntu package management system in the image.
policies.name: Ubuntu Package Manager in Image
policies.rationale: Package managers make it easier for attackers to use compromised containers, since they can easily add software.
policies.remediation: Run `dpkg -r --force-all apt apt-get && dpkg -r --force-all debconf dpkg` in the image build for production containers.

policies.description: Protect pod default service account tokens from compromise by minimizing the mounting of the default service account token to only those pods whose application requires interaction with the Kubernetes API.
policies.name: Pod Service Account Token Automatically Mounted
policies.rationale: By default, Kubernetes automatically provisions a service account for each pod and mounts the secret at runtime. This service account is not typically used. If this pod is compromised and the compromised user has access to the service account, the service account could be used to escalate privileges within the cluster. To reduce the likelihood of privilege escalation this service account should not be mounted by default unless the pod requires direct access to the Kubernetes API as part of the pods functionality.
policies.remediation: Add `automountServiceAccountToken: false` or a value distinct from 'default' for the `serviceAccountName` key to the deployment's Pod configuration.

policies.description: This policy generates a violation for any process execution that is not explicitly allowed by a locked process baseline for a given container specification within a Kubernetes deployment.
policies.name: Unauthorized Process Execution
policies.rationale: A locked process baseline communicates high confidence that execution of a process not included in the baseline positively indicates malicious activity.
policies.remediation: Evaluate this process execution for malicious intent, examine other accessible resources for abnormal activity, then kill the pod in which this process executed.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with containers escalating with CAP_SYS_ADMIN
policies.name: CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability added
policies.rationale: CAP_SYS_ADMIN grants an elevated level of privilege to a container that may not be necessary. https://lwn.net/Articles/486306/ explains what CAP_SYS_ADMIN does and points to possible alternatives.
policies.remediation: Ensure that the container really needs the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability or use a userspace derivative.

policies.description: Alert on deployments exposing port 22, commonly reserved for SSH access.
policies.name: Secure Shell (ssh) Port Exposed
policies.rationale: Port 22 is reserved for SSH access. SSH should not typically be used within containers.
policies.remediation: Ensure that non-SSH services are not using port 22. Ensure that any actual SSH servers have been vetted.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with curl present
policies.name: Curl in Image
policies.rationale: Leaving download tools like curl in an image makes it easier for attackers to use compromised containers, since they can easily download software.
policies.remediation: Use your package manager's "remove", "purge" or "erase" command to remove curl from the image build for production containers. Ensure that any configuration files are also removed.

policies.description: Alert on deployments running in privileged mode with fixable vulnerabilities with a CVSS of at least 6
policies.name: Fixable CVSS >= 6 and Privileged
policies.rationale: Known vulnerabilities make it easier for adversaries to exploit your application, and highly privileged containers pose greater risk. You can fix these high-severity vulnerabilities by updating to a newer version of the affected component(s).
policies.remediation: Use your package manager to update to a fixed version in future builds, run your container with lower privileges, or speak with your security team to mitigate the vulnerabilities.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with fixable vulnerabilities with a CVSS of at least 7
policies.name: Fixable CVSS >= 7
policies.rationale: Known vulnerabilities make it easier for adversaries to exploit your application. You can fix these high-severity vulnerabilities by updating to a newer version of the affected component(s).
policies.remediation: Use your package manager to update to a fixed version in future builds or speak with your security team to mitigate the vulnerabilities.

policies.description: Alerts if deployments are missing an egress Network Policy
policies.name: Deployments should have at least one egress Network Policy

policySections.sectionName: Alert on missing egress Network Policy

policies.rationale: Pods that lack egress Network Policies have unrestricted network access and may exfiltrate data or communicate with untrusted endpoints
policies.remediation: Create and apply an appropriate Network Policy of type egress to all Deployments. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/ for details

policies.description: Alerts if deployments are missing an ingress Network Policy
policies.name: Deployments should have at least one ingress Network Policy

policySections.sectionName: Alert on missing ingres Network Policy

policies.rationale: Pods that lack ingress Network Policies have unrestricted reachability on the network and may be exposed to attacks
policies.remediation: Create and apply an appropriate Network Policy of type ingress to all Deployments. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/ for details

policies.description: Alert on deployments with components of the Red Hat/Fedora/CentOS package management system.
policies.name: Red Hat Package Manager in Image
policies.rationale: Package managers make it easier for attackers to use compromised containers, since they can easily add software.
policies.remediation: Run `rpm -e --nodeps $(rpm -qa '*rpm*' '*dnf*' '*libsolv*' '*hawkey*' 'yum*')` in the image build for production containers.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with a volume mount on the container runtime socket
policies.name: Mount Container Runtime Socket
policies.rationale: Mounting the container runtime socket implies container access to the runtime daemon. With direct access to the runtime daemon, a user can schedule containers and collect information about the running containers. This can be used as a method of discovery or persistence in an attack. Depending on the container runtime configuration, this may also be used as a method of privilege escalation to the host operating system. Since this can be used as an attack, deployments that mount the container runtime socket should be minimized to those absolutely necessary.
policies.remediation: Investigate if this deployment is being deployed for legitimate business purposes, and if so, that mounting the container runtime socket is required. Perform one of the following actions based on this investigation: 1. Exclude the deployment in this policy because it is being deployed for legitimate use cases. 2. Do not mount the container runtime socket in the deployment and redeploy. 3. Launch an investigation into why a deployment with this insecure configuration useful to attackers was deployed.

policies.description: Alert when a deployment does not drop all capabilities.
policies.name: Drop All Capabilities
policies.rationale: Because capabilities permit privileged operations, it is a recommended best practice to drop all capabilities that a deployment can have, and then add only the capabilities that the deployment needs.
policies.remediation: Ensure that the deployment manifest has `drop: ALL` in the securityContext section of the container manifest.

policies.description: Alert on deployments missing the 'email' annotation
policies.name: Required Annotation: Email
policies.rationale: The 'email' annotation should always be specified so that issues with the deployment can quickly be routed to the proper party.
policies.remediation: Redeploy your service and set the 'email' annotation as your email or your team's email.

policies.description: Detects when the 'addgroup' or 'groupadd' binary is executed, which can be used to add a new linux group.
policies.name: Linux Group Add Execution
policies.rationale: Groups added in run time can be used to take ownership of files and processes
policies.remediation: Consider using a base image that doesn't have a shell such as SCRATCH or gcr.io/distroless. If not, modify your Dockerfile to use the exec form of CMD/ENTRYPOINT (["using braces"]) instead of the shell form (no braces)

policies.description: Detects when the 'useradd', 'adduser' or 'usermod' binary is executed, which can be used to add a new linux user.
policies.name: Linux User Add Execution
policies.rationale: Users or groups added in run time can be used to take ownership of files and processes.
policies.remediation: Consider using a base image that doesn't have a shell such as SCRATCH or gcr.io/distroless. If not, modify your Dockerfile to use the exec form of CMD/ENTRYPOINT (["using braces"]) instead of the shell form (no braces)

policies.description: Alert when the Alpine Linux package manager (apk) is executed at runtime
policies.name: Alpine Linux Package Manager Execution
policies.rationale: Use of package managers at runtime indicates that new software may be being introduced into containers while they are running.
policies.remediation: Run `apk --purge del apk-tools` in the image build for production containers. Change applications to no longer use package managers at runtime, if applicable.

policies.description: Alert when Debian/Ubuntu package manager programs are executed at runtime
policies.name: Ubuntu Package Manager Execution
policies.rationale: Use of package managers at runtime indicates that new software may be being introduced into containers while they are running.
policies.remediation: Run `dpkg -r --force-all apt && dpkg -r --force-all debconf dpkg` in the image build for production containers. Change applications to no longer use package managers at runtime, if applicable.

policies.description: Detected usage of the chkconfig service manager; typically this is not used within a container
policies.name: chkconfig Execution
policies.rationale: chkconfig can be used to activate and deactivate services, and should generally not be run within a container
policies.remediation: Consider removing the chkconfig utility, or using a base container image that doesn't have this utility in it

policies.description: Detects the usage of the crontab scheduled jobs editor
policies.name: crontab Execution
policies.rationale: Crontab running in a container with access to a shell makes it easier to 'clandestinely' schedule processes to run in order to better evade detection
policies.remediation: In Kubernetes, consider replacing your crontab with an orchestrator-native CronJob as part of Kube workload

policies.description: Alert when Red Hat/Fedora/CentOS package manager programs are executed at runtime.
policies.name: Red Hat Package Manager Execution
policies.rationale: Use of package managers at runtime indicates that new software may be being introduced into containers while they are running.
policies.remediation: Run `rpm -e --nodeps $(rpm -qa '*rpm*' '*dnf*' '*libsolv*' '*hawkey*' 'yum*')` in the image build for production containers. Change applications to no longer use package managers at runtime, if applicable.

policies.description: Alert on privileged pods that execute iptables or nftables
policies.name: Iptables or nftables Executed in Privileged Container
policies.rationale: Processes that are running with UID 0 run as the root user. iptables and nftables can be used in privileged containers to modify the node's network routing.
policies.remediation: Specify the USER instruction in the Docker image or the runAsUser field within the Pod Security Context

policies.description: Detects execution of iptables; iptables is a deprecated way of managing network state in containers
policies.name: iptables Execution
policies.rationale: iptables is a deprecated way of managing network state in containers
policies.remediation: Check for any processes that may be modifying iptables rules. Check for open ports that may be allowing code injection to modify iptables rules

policies.description: Detects execution of shell (bash/csh/sh/zsh) as a subprocess of a java application
policies.name: Shell Spawned by Java Application
policies.rationale: Java application launching a shell can be an indicator of remote code execution
policies.remediation: Determine whether this is intended behavior of the application or an indication of malicious activity

policies.description: Alert when binaries used to compile software are executed at runtime
policies.name: Compiler Tool Execution
policies.rationale: Use of compilation tools during runtime indicates that new software may be being introduced into containers while they are running.
policies.remediation: Compile all necessary application code during the image build process. Avoid packaging software build tools in container images. Use your distribution's package manager to remove compilers and other build tools from images.

policies.description: Cryptocurrency mining process spawned
policies.name: Cryptocurrency Mining Process Execution
policies.rationale: Cryptocurrency mining binaries are often evidence of malicious activity or a hijacked cluster.
policies.remediation: Ensure that the base image used to create the Dockerfile doesn't have cryptocurrency mining software packaged with it. Check for open ports that may allow for remote code execution

policies.description: Detects execution of binaries that can be used to manipulate network configuration and management.
policies.name: Network Management Execution
policies.rationale: Network management tools can be used for a variety of tasks, including mapping out your network, overwriting iptables rules, or ssh tunneling to name a few.
policies.remediation: Remove unncessary network managment tools from the container image.

policies.description: Detects execution of netcat in a container
policies.name: Netcat Execution Detected
policies.rationale: netcat is a known malicious process
policies.remediation: Consider removing package managers during the build process that could be used to download such software. Check that exposed ports don't allow for remote code execution

policies.description: Alerts when the nmap process launches in a container during run time
policies.name: nmap Execution
policies.rationale: Nmap can be used to probe a running container's network to enumerate open ports and perform other actions such as OS version detection and launching over-the-network scripted attacks
policies.remediation: Consider removing package managers during the build process that could be used to download such software. Check that exposed ports don't allow for remote code execution

policies.description: Alert on deployments that execute a remote file copy tool
policies.name: Remote File Copy Binary Execution
policies.rationale: Remote copy tools can be used to exfiltrate data from a container
policies.remediation: Remove tools like scp, sshfs, ssh-copy-id, etc. from your image and redeploy it

policies.description: Detects container running the SSH daemon
policies.name: Secure Shell Server (sshd) Execution
policies.rationale: The secure shell server allows shell access to a container, which can be dangerous.
policies.remediation: If ssh is absolutely required, ensure that it is not using default authentication. Otherwise, consider removing it from the container altogether.

policies.description: Detected usage of the systemctl service manager
policies.name: systemctl Execution
policies.rationale: The systemctl service manager is generally not used in containers, and its use could indicate suspicious activity
policies.remediation: Remove systemctl from the image before deploying, or consider using a base image that doesn't bundle systemctl

policies.description: Detected usage of the systemd service manager
policies.name: systemd Execution
policies.rationale: The systemd service manager is generally not used in containers, and its use could indicate suspicious activity
policies.remediation: Remove systemd from the image before deploying, or consider using a base image that doesn't bundle systemd

policies.description: Detects misuse of the healthz/kubelet API/heapster endpoint
policies.name: Process Targeting Cluster Kubelet Endpoint
policies.rationale: A pod communicating to a Kubernetes API from via command line is highly irregular
policies.remediation: Look for open ports that may allow remote execution. Remove network utilities like curl and wget that allow these connections. Consider a firewall deny ingress firewall rule to the node serving the API

policies.description: Detects misuse of the Kubernetes docker stats endpoint
policies.name: Process Targeting Cluster Kubernetes Docker Stats Endpoint
policies.rationale: A pod communicating to a Kubernetes API from via command line is highly irregular
policies.remediation: Look for open ports that may allow remote execution. Remove network utilities like curl and wget that allow these connections. Consider a firewall deny ingress firewall rule to the node serving the API

policies.description: Detects misuse of the Kubernetes Service API endpoint
policies.name: Process Targeting Kubernetes Service Endpoint
policies.rationale: A pod communicating to a Kubernetes API from via command line is highly irregular
policies.remediation: Look for open ports that may allow remote execution. Remove network utilities like curl and wget that allow these connections. Consider a firewall deny ingress firewall rule to the node serving the API

policies.description: Deployments with externally exposed endpoints represent a higher risk
policies.name: Deployments with externally exposed endpoints
policies.rationale: Deployments with services exposed outside the cluster are at a higher risk of attempted intrusions because they are reachable outside of the cluster.
policies.remediation: Verify that service exposure outside of the cluster is required. If the service is only needed for intra-cluster communication, use service type ClusterIP.

policies.description: Images should be scanned frequently for any vulnerabilities. You should rebuild all images to include these patches and then instantiate new containers from them.
policies.name: Docker CIS 4.4: Ensure images are scanned and rebuilt to include security patches
policies.rationale: Vulnerabilities are loopholes or bugs that can be exploited by hackers or malicious users, and security patches are updates to resolve these vulnerabilities. Image vulnerability scanning tools can be use to find vulnerabilities in images and then check for available patches to mitigate these. Patches update the system to a more recent code base which does not contain these problems, and being on a supported version of the code base is very important, as vendors do not tend to supply patches for older versions which have gone out of support. Security patches should be evaluated before applying and patching should be implemented in line with the organization's IT Security Policy. Care should be taken with the results returned by vulnerability assessment tools, as some will simply return results based on software banners, and these may not be entirely accurate.
policies.remediation: Images should be re-built ensuring that the latest version of the base images are used, to keep the operating system patch level at an appropriate level. Once the images have been re-built, containers should be re-started making use of the updated images.

policies.description: IPC (POSIX/SysV IPC) namespace provides separation of named shared memory segments, semaphores and message queues. The IPC namespace on the host should therefore not be shared with containers and should remain isolated.
policies.name: Docker CIS 5.16: Ensure that the host's IPC namespace is not shared
policies.rationale: The IPC namespace provides separation of IPC between the host and containers. If the host's IPC namespace is shared with the container, it would allow processes within the container to see all of IPC communications on the host system. This would remove the benefit of IPC level isolation between host and containers. An attacker with access to a container could get access to the host at this level with major consequences. The IPC namespace should therefore not be shared between the host and its containers.
policies.remediation: You should not create a deployment with `hostIPC: true`

policies.description: When HostNetwork is enabled the container is not placed inside a separate network stack. The container's networking is not containerized when this option is applied. The consequence of this is that the container has full access to the host's network interfaces. It also enables a shared UTS namespace. The UTS namespace provides isolation between two system identifiers: the hostname and the NIS domain name. It is used to set the hostname and the domain which are visible to running processes in that namespace. Processes running within containers do not typically require to know either the hostname or the domain name. The UTS namespace should therefore not be shared with the host.
policies.name: Docker CIS 5.9 and 5.20: Ensure that the host's network namespace is not shared
policies.rationale: Selecting this option is potentially dangerous. It allows the container process to open reserved low numbered ports in the way that any other root process can. It also allows the container to access network services such as D-bus on a Docker host. A container process could potentially carry out undesired actions, such as shutting down the host. The container will also share the network namespace with the host, providing full permission for each container to change the hostname of the host. This is not in line with good security practice and should not be permitted.
policies.remediation: You should not create a deployment with `hostNetwork: true`

policies.description: The Process ID (PID) namespace isolates the process ID space, meaning that processes in different PID namespaces can have the same PID. This creates process level isolation between the containers and the host.
policies.name: Docker CIS 5.15: Ensure that the host's process namespace is not shared
policies.rationale: PID namespace provides separation between processes. It prevents system processes from being visible, and allows process ids to be reused including PID 1. If the host's PID namespace is shared with containers, it would basically allow these to see all of the processes on the host system. This reduces the benefit of process level isolation between the host and the containers. Under these circumstances a malicious user who has access to a container could get access to processes on the host itself, manipulate them, and even be able to kill them. This could allow for the host itself being shut down, which could be extremely serious, particularly in a multi-tenanted environment. You should not share the host's process namespace with the containers running on it.
policies.remediation: You should not create a deployment with `hostPID: true`

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images that haven't been updated in 90 days
policies.name: 90-Day Image Age
policies.rationale: Base images are updated frequently with bug fixes and vulnerability patches. Image age exceeding 90 days may indicate a higher risk of vulnerabilities existing in the image.
policies.remediation: Rebuild your image, push a new minor version (with a new immutable tag), and update your service to use it.

policies.description: Alert on deployments exposing port 22, commonly reserved for SSH access.
policies.name: Secure Shell (ssh) Port Exposed in Image
policies.rationale: Port 22 is reserved for SSH access. SSH should not typically be used within containers.
policies.remediation: Ensure that non-SSH services are not using port 22. Ensure that any actual SSH servers have been vetted.

policies.description: Alert when user impersonation is used to access a secret within the cluster.
policies.name: OpenShift: Kubernetes Secret Accessed by an Impersonated User
policies.rationale: Users with impersonation access allows users to invoke any command as a different user, typically for troubleshooting purposes (i.e using the oc --as command). This may be used to bypass existing security controls such as RBAC.
policies.remediation: Audit usage of impersonation when accessing secrets to ensure this access is used for valid business purposes.

policies.description: Alert on deployments using 'insecure' in the command
policies.name: Insecure specified in CMD
policies.rationale: Using insecure in a command implies accessing or providing data from a server on an unencrypted connection.
policies.remediation: Use a certificate manager and certificate rotation routinely to ensure secure service-to-service communication.

policies.description: Alert on the presence of the Kubernetes dashboard service
policies.name: Kubernetes Dashboard Deployed
policies.rationale: The Kubernetes dashboard can be used to gain external access to a cluster, or to obtain additional access once inside.
policies.remediation: Modify your cluster configuration to disable the Kubernetes dashboard service if it is not in use. In Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), you can execute: gcloud container clusters update --update-addons=KubernetesDashboard=DISABLED [cluster-name]

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images using tag 'latest'
policies.name: Latest tag
policies.rationale: Using latest tag can result in running heterogeneous versions of code. Many Docker hosts cache the Docker images, which means newer versions of the latest tag will not be picked up. See https://docs.docker.com/develop/dev-best-practices for more best practices.
policies.remediation: Consider moving to semantic versioning based on code releases (semver.org) or using the first 12 characters of the source control SHA. This will allow you to tie the Docker image to the code.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images containing the Log4Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-44228 and CVE-2021-45046). There are flaws in the Java logging library Apache Log4j in versions from 2.0-beta9 to 2.15.0, excluding 2.12.2.
policies.name: Log4Shell: log4j Remote Code Execution vulnerability
policies.rationale: These vulnerabilities allows a remote attacker to execute code on the server if the system logs an attacker-controlled string value with the attacker's JNDI LDAP server lookup.
policies.remediation: Update the log4j libary to version 2.16.0 (for Java 8 or later), 2.12.2 (for Java 7) or later. If not possible to upgrade, then remove the JndiLookup class from the classpath: zip -q -d log4j-core-*.jar org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class

policies.description: Processes that indicate login attempts
policies.name: Login Binaries
policies.rationale: Login processes at runtime are unusual in a container
policies.remediation: Ensure that the base image used to create the Dockerfile doesn't have login binaries packaged with it.

policies.description: Mount propagation mode allows mounting container volumes in Bidirectional, Host to Container, and None modes. Do not use Bidirectional mount propagation mode unless explicitly needed.
policies.name: Docker CIS 5.19: Ensure mount propagation mode is not enabled
policies.rationale: A Bidirectional mount is replicated at all mounts and changes made at any mount point are propagated to all other mount points. Mounting a volume in Bidirectional mode does not restrict any other container from mounting and making changes to that volume. As this is likely not a desirable option from a security standpoint, this feature should not be used unless explicitly required
policies.remediation: Do not mount volumes in Bidirectional propagation mode.

policies.description: This policy generates a violation for the network flows that fall outside baselines for which 'alert on anomalous violations' is set.
policies.name: Unauthorized Network Flow
policies.rationale: The network baseline is a list of flows that are allowed, and once it is frozen, any flow outside that is a concern.
policies.remediation: Evaluate this network flow. If deemed to be okay, add it to the baseline. If not, investigate further as required.

policies.description: AppArmor is an effective and easy-to-use Linux application security system. It is available on some Linux distributions by default, for example, on Debian and Ubuntu.
policies.name: Docker CIS 5.1 Ensure that, if applicable, an AppArmor Profile is enabled
policies.rationale: AppArmor protects the Linux OS and applications from various threats by enforcing a security policy which is also known as an AppArmor profile. You can create your own AppArmor profile for containers or use Docker's default profile. Enabling this feature enforces security policies on containers as defined in the profile.
policies.remediation: If AppArmor is applicable for your Linux OS, you should enable it.  Verify AppArmor is installed, create or import an AppArmor profile for your containers, enable enforcement of the policy, and add the appropriate AppArmor annotations to your deployment.

policies.description: Alert on deployments that have containers without CPU request or memory limit
policies.name: No CPU request or memory limit specified
policies.rationale: A container without a specified CPU request may be starved for CPU time, while a container without a specified memory limit may cause the host to become over-provisioned.
policies.remediation: Specify CPU request and memory limit for your deployment.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images that have not been scanned
policies.name: Images with no scans
policies.rationale: Without a scan, there will be no vulnerability information for this image
policies.remediation: Configure the appropriate registry and scanner integrations so that StackRox can obtain scans for your images.

policies.description: Seccomp filtering provides a means to filter incoming system calls. The default seccomp profile uses an allow list to permit a large number of common system calls, and block all others.
policies.name: Docker CIS 5.21: Ensure the default seccomp profile is not disabled
policies.rationale: A large number of system calls are exposed to every userland process with many of them going unused for the entire lifetime of the process. Most of applications do not need all these system calls and would therefore benefit from having a reduced set of available system calls. Having a reduced set of system calls reduces the total kernel surface exposed to the application and thus improvises application security.
policies.remediation: By default, seccomp profiles are enabled. You do not need to do anything unless you want to modify and use a modified seccomp profile.

policies.description: Alert on deployments missing the 'owner' or 'team' annotation
policies.name: Required Annotation: Owner/Team
policies.rationale: The 'owner' or 'team' annotation should always be specified so that the deployment can quickly be associated with a specific user or team.
policies.remediation: Redeploy your service and set the 'owner' or 'team' annotation to yourself or your team respectively per organizational standards.

policies.description: Alert on deployments missing the 'owner' or 'team' label
policies.name: Required Label: Owner/Team
policies.rationale: The 'owner' or 'team' label should always be specified so that the deployment can quickly be associated with a specific user or team.
policies.remediation: Redeploy your service and set the 'owner' or 'team' label to yourself or your team respectively per organizational standards.

policies.description: Processes that indicate attempts to change passwd
policies.name: Password Binaries
policies.rationale: Attempts to change password during runtime in containers is unusual
policies.remediation: Ensure that the base image used to create the Dockerfile doesn't have passwd binaries packaged with it.

policies.description: Alerts when Kubernetes API receives request to attach to a container
policies.name: Kubernetes Actions: Attach to Pod
policies.rationale: 'pods/attach' is non-standard approach for interacting with containers. Attackers with permissions could execute malicious code and compromise resources within a cluster
policies.remediation: Restrict RBAC access to the 'pods/attach' resource according to the Principle of Least Privilege. Limit such usage only to development, testing or debugging (non-production) activities

policies.description: Alerts when Kubernetes API receives request to execute command in container
policies.name: Kubernetes Actions: Exec into Pod
policies.rationale: 'pods/exec' is non-standard approach for interacting with containers. Attackers with permissions could execute malicious code and compromise resources within a cluster
policies.remediation: Restrict RBAC access to the 'pods/exec' resource according to the Principle of Least Privilege. Limit such usage only to development, testing or debugging (non-production) activities

policies.description: Alerts when Kubernetes API receives port forward request
policies.name: Kubernetes Actions: Port Forward to Pod
policies.rationale: 'pods/portforward' is non-standard way to access applications running on Kubernetes. Attackers with permissions could gain access to application and compromise it
policies.remediation: Restrict RBAC access to the 'pods/portforward' resource according to the Principle of Least Privilege. Limit exposing application through port forwarding only development, testing or debugging (non-production) activities. For external traffic, expose application through a LoadBalancer/NodePort service or Ingress Controller

policies.description: Alerts if a deployment has containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation set to true in its security context.
policies.name: Container with privilege escalation allowed
policies.rationale: A container process can run with more privileges than its parent process if the container's security context has the boolean setting allowPrivilegeEscalation enabled. In Kubernetes pods, this setting is true by default. Set the value to false if the pod is to run as a non-root user.
policies.remediation: Verify that privileged escalation is required and cannot be provided with a subset of other controls. Disable privilege escalation by setting allowPrivilegeEscalation to false.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with containers running in privileged mode
policies.name: Privileged Container
policies.rationale: Containers running as privileged represent greater post-exploitation risk by allowing an attacker to access all host devices, run a daemon in the container, etc.
policies.remediation: Verify that privileged capabilities are required and cannot be provided with a subset of other controls.

policies.description: Alert on deployments that contain processes running with UID 0
policies.name: Process with UID 0
policies.rationale: Processes that are running with UID 0 run as the root user. This can allow for unintended privilege escalation if a container mounts host directories that are owned by the host's root user
policies.remediation: Specify the USER instruction in the Docker image or the runAsUser field within the Pod Security Context

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images containing components that are susceptible to a Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability for HTTP/2 servers.
policies.name: Rapid Reset: Denial of Service Vulnerability in HTTP/2 Protocol
policies.rationale: This is a flaw in the handling of multiplexed streams in http/2. A client can rapidly create a request and immediately reset them, which creates extra work for the server while avoiding hitting any server-side limits, resulting in a denial of service attack.
policies.remediation: Upgrade vulnerable components or images to the latest version.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with containers with read-write root filesystem
policies.name: Container using read-write root filesystem
policies.rationale: Containers running with read-write root filesystem represent greater post-exploitation risk by allowing an attacker to modify important files in the container.
policies.remediation: Use a read-only root filesystem, and use volume mounts to allow writes to specific sub-directories depending on your application's needs.

policies.description: Alert when Red Hat images are not digitally signed by Red Hat
policies.name: Red Hat images must be signed by a Red Hat release key

policySections.sectionName: All images in certain Red Hat registries must be signed by Red Hat
All images in selected Red Hat owned quay.io remotes must be signed by Red Hat

policies.rationale: Red Hat images should be signed using Red Hat's Cosign product signing keys (https://access.redhat.com/security/team/key). Older OpenShift images that predate the introduction of Cosign signatures may not be signed.
policies.remediation: Confirm the authenticity of the image by reaching out to Red Hat support.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images missing the specified label.
policies.name: Required Image Label
policies.rationale: Only images with the specified label should be deployed to ensure all deployments contain approved images.
policies.remediation: Request that the maintainer add the required label to the image.

policies.description: The TCP/IP port numbers below 1024 are considered privileged ports. Normal users and processes are not allowed to use them for various security reasons. Containers are, however, allowed to map their ports to privileged ports.
policies.name: Docker CIS 5.7: Ensure privileged ports are not mapped within containers
policies.rationale: By default, if the user does not specifically declare a container port to host port mapping, the containers ports will be mapped to available non-privileged host ports. Containers are, however, allow to map their ports to a privileged ports on the host if the user explicitly declares it. In Docker this is because containers are executed with NET_BIND_SERVICE Linux kernel capability which does not restrict privileged port mapping. The privileged ports receive and transmit various pieces of data which are security sensitive and allowing containers to use them is not in line with good security practice.
policies.remediation: You should not map container ports to privileged host ports when starting a container. You should also, ensure that there is no such container to host privileged port mapping declarations in the Dockerfile.

policies.description: Containers should run as a non-root user
policies.name: Docker CIS 4.1: Ensure That a User for the Container Has Been Created
policies.rationale: It is good practice to run the container as a non-root user, where possible. This can be done via the USER directive in the Dockerfile. You can exclude this policy from OpenShift clusters because they run containers using an arbitrarily assigned user ID by default.
policies.remediation: Ensure that the Dockerfile for each container switches from the root user

policies.description: Alert on deployments that use a Dockerfile with 'VOLUME /run/secrets'
policies.name: Improper Usage of Orchestrator Secrets Volume
policies.rationale: /run/secrets is a path for secrets that gets populated by the orchestrator. Volumes should not be used for secrets, and data mounts should have a separate mount path.
policies.remediation: Mount the volume to a different path. If secrets are stored in the volume, utilize the orchestrator secrets or your security team's secret management solution instead.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images that haven't been scanned in 30 days
policies.name: 30-Day Scan Age
policies.rationale: Out-of-date scans may not identify the most recent CVEs.
policies.remediation: Integrate a scanner with the StackRox Kubernetes Security Platform to trigger scans automatically.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with environment variables that contain 'SECRET'
policies.name: Environment Variable Contains Secret
policies.rationale: Using secrets in environment variables may allow inspection into your secrets from the host or even through the orchestrator UI.
policies.remediation: Migrate your secrets from environment variables to orchestrator secrets or your security team's secret management solution.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with Kubernetes secret mounted as environment variable
policies.name: Secret Mounted as Environment Variable
policies.rationale: Using secrets in environment variables may allow inspection into your secrets from the host.
policies.remediation: Migrate your secrets from environment variables to your security team's secret management solution.

policies.description: Alert on deployments mounting sensitive host directories
policies.name: Mounting Sensitive Host Directories
policies.rationale: Mounting system directories from host implies container access to sensitive files on the host. This expands the attack surface of the container and gives an intruder an opportunity to break containment if the host is not properly secured.
policies.remediation: Ensure that deployments do not mount sensitive host directories, or exclude this deployment if host mount is required.

policies.description: Processes that are known to use setuid binaries
policies.name: SetUID Processes
policies.rationale: setuid permits users to run certain programs with escalated privileges
policies.remediation: Ensure that the base image used to create the Dockerfile doesn't have setuid software packaged with it.

policies.description: Alert on containers running in privileged mode with important or critical fixable vulnerabilities
policies.name: Privileged Containers with Important and Critical Fixable CVEs
policies.rationale: Known vulnerabilities make it easier for adversaries to exploit your application, and highly-privileged containers pose greater risk. You can fix these high-severity vulnerabilities by updating to a newer version of the affected component(s).
policies.remediation: Use your package manager to update to a fixed version in future builds, run your container with lower privileges, or speak with your security team to mitigate the vulnerabilities.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with fixable vulnerabilities with a Severity Rating at least Important
policies.name: Fixable Severity at least Important
policies.rationale: Known vulnerabilities make it easier for adversaries to exploit your application. You can fix these high-severity vulnerabilities by updating to a newer version of the affected component(s).
policies.remediation: Use your package manager to update to a fixed version in future builds or speak with your security team to mitigate the vulnerabilities.

policies.description: Processes that indicate attempts to modify shadow files
policies.name: Shadow File Modification
policies.rationale: Attempts to change shadow file during runtime in containers is unusual
policies.remediation: Ensure that the base image used to create the Dockerfile doesn't have shadow utils packaged with it.

policies.description: Commands that are used to add/remove a shell
policies.name: Shell Management
policies.rationale: Shell management is not usually done at runtime
policies.remediation: Ensure that the base image used to create the Dockerfile doesn't have shell binaries packaged with it.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images containing Spring4Shell vulnerability CVE-2022-22965 which affects the Spring MVC component and vulnerability CVE-2022-22963 which affects the Spring Cloud component. There are flaws in Spring Cloud Function (versions 3.1.6, 3.2.2 and older unsupported versions) and in Spring Framework (5.3.0 to 5.3.17, 5.2.0 to 5.2.19 and older unsupported versions).
policies.name: Spring4Shell (Spring Framework Remote Code Execution) and Spring Cloud Function vulnerabilities
policies.rationale: In Spring Cloud Function, when using routing functionality, a user can provide a specially crafted SpEL as a routing-expression that may result in remote code execution (RCE) and access to local resources. For Spring Framework, a Spring MVC or Spring WebFlux application running on JDK 9+ may be vulnerable to RCE via data binding.
policies.remediation: Upgrade Spring Cloud Function to version 3.1.7 or 3.2.3. Upgrade Spring Framework to version 5.3.18+ (if currently on 5.3.x) or 5.2.20+ (if currently on 5.2.x). If not possible to upgrade Spring Framework, then apply an appropriate workaround from the suggested workarounds on https://spring.io/blog/2022/03/31/spring-framework-rce-early-announcement

policies.description: Alert on deployments with images containing Apache Struts vulnerability CVE-2017-5638
policies.name: Apache Struts: CVE-2017-5638
policies.rationale: CVE-2017-5638 is a serious and easily-exploitable vulnerability in Apache Struts.
policies.remediation: Rebuild your container with an updated version of Apache Struts.

policies.description: Ensure update instructions are not used alone in the Dockerfile
policies.name: Docker CIS 4.7: Alert on Update Instruction
policies.rationale: Adding update instructions in a single line on the Dockerfile will cause the update layer to be cached. When you then build any image later using the same instruction, this will cause the previously cached update layer to be used, potentially preventing any fresh updates from being applied to later builds.
policies.remediation: Use update instructions together with install instructions and version pinning for packages while installing them. This prevents caching and forces the extraction of the required versions.

policies.description: Alert on deployments with wget present
policies.name: Wget in Image
policies.rationale: Leaving download tools like wget in an image makes it easier for attackers to use compromised containers, since they can easily download software.
policies.remediation: Use your package manager's "remove" command to remove wget from the image build for production containers.
